passages.quote: Kodera site: stakes are driven obliquely and logs laid on the row; stakes are then driven again, obliquely or vertically, to fix the logs. Repeating this produces an A-frame form. passages.original: 古照遣跡 杭を斜めに打ち込んで丸太をこの列上に置いたのち、丸太を固定するために再び杭を斜めや垂直に打ち込む。こうした作業をくり返すことによって合掌形式としている。木組みのいくつかの個所はフジづるでしばり、すき間には粘土や礫などをつめ、草などの編物で押さえて堰き止め、水位を上昇させる機能を高めている。

footnotes.assertion: At Kodera the stakes were driven at a slant, logs laid along them and more stakes driven to hold the logs, the joints tied with wisteria vine and the gaps packed with clay and gravel.

passages.quote: [Earliest examples] "The Asuka River - if one laid a shigarami across it and dammed it, would even the flowing water go gently?" (Man'yoshu (late 8th century) 2.197) "at the meeting of the two rivers they cut great trees and laid them as an abatis, and heaped up shigarami in great number" (Heike monogatari (early 13th century) 7)
passages.original: [初出の実例]「明日香川四我良美(シガラミ)渡し塞(せ)かませば流るる水ものどにかあらまし」(出典：万葉集（８Ｃ後）二・一九七) 「二の河の落ちあひに大木をきってさかもぎにひき、しがらみを夥しうかきあげたれば」(出典：平家物語（１３Ｃ前）七)

footnotes.assertion: The word's earliest written examples are a poem of the eighth-century Man'yoshu, which imagines one laid across the Asuka River to dam it, and the Heike monogatari of the early thirteenth century, where one is heaped up as a work of war.
footnotes.question: 0059-where-the-ditch-leaves-the-brook-the-intake-and-its-weir-toshuko-and-seki.html

passages.quote: In Kanoya city on the Osumi peninsula of Kagoshima prefecture there survives a 'brushwood weir' (shibaizeki), which uses the scrub trees growing on the hills and fields to take water for farming.
passages.original: 鹿児島県大隅半島の鹿屋（かのや）市には、農業用水をとるために山野に生えている雑木を用いた「柴井堰（しばいぜき）」が残る。

passages.quote: The Kawaharazono weir (kawaharazono izeki), on the lower Kushira River, is a somewhat unusual weir.
passages.original: 串良川（くしらがわ）下流域にある川原園井堰（かわはらぞのいぜき）は少し変わった堰だ。

passages.quote: The weir was built here in the early Edo period. It began with the new-field development by the Satsuma domain that started about 380 years ago. It is handed down that at first it was either a stone weir or plants woven onto a foundation of wooden stakes.
passages.original: ここに堰がつくられたのは江戸時代初期。380年ほど前に始まった薩摩藩による新田開発に端を発する。当初は石堰だったとも、木杭の基礎に草木を編み込んだものだったとも伝わる。

passages.quote: Built every year in March; in September, when the rice harvest is over, only half is taken down, and the next year the brushwood is laid anew
passages.original: 毎年3月に築き、稲刈りが終わる9月に半分だけ撤去して、翌年は新たに柴架けをする

passages.quote: In 1902 (Meiji 35) the foundation became stone, but it was often washed away by typhoons, so in 1950 (Showa 25) a concrete foundation was made.
passages.original: 1902年（明治35）に基礎は石となったが台風でしばしば流されたため、1950年（昭和25）にコンクリート製の基礎がつくられた。

footnotes.assertion: Its brushwood is still laid anew every March, though the weir has stood on a concrete foundation since 1950.
footnotes.question: 0059-where-the-ditch-leaves-the-brook-the-intake-and-its-weir-toshuko-and-seki.html

passages.quote: Grass weir: where an agreement with downstream users prevents building a permanent weir, a simple weir of driven stakes with kaya woven between them is still used today (Chiyoda, Saga).
passages.original: 草堰 下流との申し合わせにより、恒久的な堰がつくれない所では、杭を打ち、その間にカヤを編みこんだ簡単な堰が今でも使われている。(佐賀県千代田町)

footnotes.assertion: Were stake weirs woven with reed before Japan began to modernize in 1868?A weir of driven stakes with reed (kaya) woven between them - the grass weir - is still used today at Chiyoda, in Saga, where an agreement with the users downstream rules out a permanent weir.
footnotes.question: 0059-where-the-ditch-leaves-the-brook-the-intake-and-its-weir-toshuko-and-seki.html

passages.quote: Weirs of the Edo period were almost all for obtaining farm water, and according to the Kenrei Shuchi they can be broadly divided into grass weirs and washing weirs.
passages.original: 江戸期のせきは農業用水の取得のためのものがほとんどであり，《県令須知》によれば草ぜきと洗いぜきに大別しうる。

footnotes.assertion: An official handbook divides the Edo-period weirs, almost all built for farm water, into grass weirs and washing weirs, without saying what either was made of.
footnotes.question: 0059-where-the-ditch-leaves-the-brook-the-intake-and-its-weir-toshuko-and-seki.html

footnotes.assertion: What the premodern record weaves into the stakes is brushwood and bamboo; a weave of reed we found only in the present-day Saga weir.
footnotes.question: 0059-where-the-ditch-leaves-the-brook-the-intake-and-its-weir-toshuko-and-seki.html

passages.quote: For these, ox-frames (ushiwaku), gabions (jakago), brushwood works (sodako) and the like were used singly, or combined and then covered with earth and gravel. For example the Tatai weir on the Takahashi River in Okayama Prefecture (built 1183) consists of a bottom frame and an upper frame of timber packed with stone, and is an oblique weir closing the whole river, about 230 m long. The upper frame at the thalweg was removed in the non-irrigation season for flood countermeasures and to sweep out sediment, and was installed anew every year in the irrigation season.
passages.original: これには、牛枠・蛇籠・そだ工などを用いてそれぞれ単独に使用したり、これらを組合わせてさらに土砂・礫を被覆したものがある。例えば、岡山県高梁川湛井堰（1183年築造）は、木枠に詰石した底枠と上枠からなり、延長約230mの全川締切り斜め堰である。ミオ筋部の上枠は非かんがい期には洪水対策・土砂掃流の目的で撤去し、かんがい期に毎年設置していた。

footnotes.assertion: The Tatai weir on the Takahashi River, built in 1183, was of timber frames packed with stone, an oblique weir about 230 m (~755 ft) long closing the whole river; the upper frame at its deep channel was taken out after each irrigation season and set in anew each year.
footnotes.question: 0059-where-the-ditch-leaves-the-brook-the-intake-and-its-weir-toshuko-and-seki.html

passages.quote: Many of the weirs of old were 'oblique weirs', extended long in the diagonally upstream direction from the intake mouth.
passages.original: 古来の堰の多くは取水口から斜め上流方向に長く延ばした「斜め堰」であった。
passages.why: a PDF - no text layer can be read here

passages.quote: An oblique weir avoids the depth of the pool and dams the riffle where the bed has become shallow, leading water to the intake mouth. At flood time the weir lies at a position off the high-velocity zone, so it also has the advantage of being hard to destroy.
passages.original: 斜め堰は，淵の深みを避け河床が浅くなった瀬を堰き止めて取水口に導く。洪水時には高流速域を外した位置に堰があるので，破壊されにくいという利点も持っている。
passages.why: a PDF - no text layer can be read here

footnotes.assertion: Many old weirs ran obliquely upstream from the intake mouth.An oblique weir, "extended long in the diagonally upstream direction from the intake mouth", dams the shallow riffle rather than the deep pool, and stands off the fastest water in a flood, so it is hard to destroy.
footnotes.question: 0059-where-the-ditch-leaves-the-brook-the-intake-and-its-weir-toshuko-and-seki.html

passages.quote: Weirs of this kind were also built in the Edo period; there were weirs made of ushi-waku and waku, and weirs of stone and of kaya-haguchi.
passages.original: このような堰は江戸時代にもつくられており、牛枠や枠でつくられた堰、石や萱羽口の堰などもありました。

passages.quote: Ushi and waku together are sometimes called ushi-waku, but the ushi has its own types (see Figure 5).
passages.original: 牛と枠は両方合わせて牛枠という場合もあるが、牛は牛でちゃんと種類（図－５参照）があり

passages.quote: Kinds of bank protection include turf and brushwood, but what Figure 7 shows is a method called kaya-haguchi.
passages.original: 護岸の種類としては芝付けや粗朶などがありますが、図－7に示しているものは萱羽口という工法です。

footnotes.assertion: The weirs of large rivers in the Edo period were timber frames weighted with stone.Diversion weirs of the Edo period were made of timber frames, of stone, and of kaya-haguchi, a bank-protection work named for its reed,
footnotes.question: 0059-where-the-ditch-leaves-the-brook-the-intake-and-its-weir-toshuko-and-seki.html

passages.quote: A waku is timber joined with mortise and tenon, not woven, built as a four-sided frame, set in the river and fixed by throwing stones in from above.
passages.original: 枠というのは、木にほぞを組み、編んだりせず、四方形を組んで川に入れ、上から石を投げ込んで固定します。

footnotes.assertion: The weirs of large rivers in the Edo period were timber frames weighted with stone.Diversion weirs of the Edo period were made of timber frames, of stone, and of kaya-haguchi, a bank-protection work named for its reed, a frame being timber joined with mortise and tenon into a square, set in the river and fixed by stones thrown in from above.
footnotes.question: 0059-where-the-ditch-leaves-the-brook-the-intake-and-its-weir-toshuko-and-seki.html

passages.quote: A cylindrical basket woven of bamboo, wire or the like, packed with cobbles or rubble. The baskets are mostly about 40-60 cm in diameter and 4-10 m long.
passages.original: 竹や鉄線などで編んだ円筒形の籠の中に玉石(たまいし)や栗石(くりいし)を詰め込んだもの。籠の大きさは直径40～60センチメートル、長さ4～10メートル程度のものが多い。

footnotes.assertion: A gabion is a long basket of stones about 40 to 60 cm (~16-24 in) across.It is "a cylindrical basket woven of bamboo, wire or the like, packed with cobbles or rubble", mostly about 40-60 cm (~16-24 in) in diameter and 4-10 m (~13-33 ft) long.
footnotes.question: 0059-where-the-ditch-leaves-the-brook-the-intake-and-its-weir-toshuko-and-seki.html

passages.quote: A coarsely woven oblong basket of bamboo or iron wire, filled with rubble, crushed stone and the like. Used in river bank-protection works to hold back soil, control the current and so on. So called because its shape resembles a great serpent lying down. Also 'stone basket'; also 'jako'. [Japanese-Portuguese Dictionary (1603-04)]
passages.original: 中に栗石、砕石などを詰めた、粗く編んだ長円形の竹または鉄線製の籠。河川の護岸工事で、土砂の防止、水流制御などに用いる。その形が、大蛇の伏している姿に似ているところからいう。石籠。じゃこ。〔日葡辞書（1603‐04）〕

footnotes.assertion: The word is in the Japanese-Portuguese dictionary of 1603-04.
footnotes.question: 0059-where-the-ditch-leaves-the-brook-the-intake-and-its-weir-toshuko-and-seki.html

passages.quote: One of the structures used for bank protection and groynes on coasts and rivers.
passages.original: 海岸・河川の護岸，水制に用いる工作物の一つ。

passages.quote: Laid in rows on the face and toe of an embankment, used as bank facing and as toe protection.
passages.original: 堤防の法面(のりめん)や法先(のりさき)に並べて置き、護岸の法覆工(のりおおいこう)や根固め工として用いられる。

passages.quote: To keep them from being washed away, long thin baskets woven of bamboo or wire and packed with stone (called jakago) and the like are used as weights.
passages.original: 流されるのを防ぐため，竹や鉄線で細長く編んだ籠に石をつめたもの(蛇籠という)などを重石として用いる。

footnotes.assertion: Were gabions laid across small streams?The sources give them for bank protection, for groynes and as weights on river frames,

footnotes.assertion: Were gabions laid across small streams?The sources give them for bank protection, for groynes and as weights on river frames, and the only gabions we found damming water were on large rivers.

footnotes.assertion: How thick was a village weir?No source we read gives the thickness or cross-section of a village weir; the only dimensions found are of river works, frames many meters long.
